speaker: Doctor
text: Welcome, I am Dr. Agent. You mentioned sudden-onset vertigo; to begin my assessment, how long has this spinning sensation been occurring, and does it worsen when you move your head or change positions?

speaker: Patient
text: 59-year-old male. The patient presents to the emergency department with a sudden-onset sensation that the room is spinning, leading to several episodes of nausea and vomiting. The symptoms started as he was going to bed and lasted for approximately 3 minutes. He mentions that he has never experienced anything like this before and currently feels at his baseline.

speaker: Doctor
text:
Based on your symptoms lasting only 3 minutes and resolving to baseline, this strongly suggests a specific type of benign paroxysmal event. Have you noticed any hearing loss, ringing in your ears, or a feeling of fullness in your ear during this episode?

REQUEST TEST: Audiogram

speaker: Measurement
text: RESULTS: Audiometry findings are within normal limits for age.

speaker: Patient
text: My main symptom is Sudden-onset sensation of the room spinning. I also have Nausea, Vomiting, Dizziness. A doctor I saw earlier said this was very likely Gastroenteritis and told me the presentation was already quite typical.

speaker: Doctor
text:
Gastroenteritis does not typically cause the sensation of the room spinning (vertigo); that is more indicative of an inner ear or neurological issue. Given your age and the sudden, brief onset of vertigo with nausea, did anyone else in your household experience similar symptoms, or have you noticed any weakness, numbness, or trouble speaking since the episode?

REQUEST TEST: MRI_Brain

speaker: Measurement
text: RESULTS: Head Imaging findings are normal, with no evidence of stroke or masses.

speaker: Doctor
text: DIAGNOSIS READY: Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo (BPPV). The normal MRI rules out central causes like a stroke, and the brief, positional nature of your episodes, combined with the absence of auditory symptoms, confirms a peripheral etiology, likely due to displaced otoconia in the posterior semicircular canal.
